research.abstract: Abstract Biological interactions involving host-associated fungi are driven by chemistry shaped over evolutionary time. For antagonistic fungi, specialization often involves acquiring genes for novel secretions—including proteins and specialized metabolites—that mediate nutrient acquisition and host defense interactions. Here, we conducted a phylogenomic investigation of Sympodiorosea, ascomycetes commonly found in basal fungus-growing ant gardens. While Sympodiorosea and related genera (Escovopsis, Luteomyces, Manidigitorum, Escovopsioides) are canonically viewed as virulent mycoparasites, non-virulent species may also emerge within these attine-associated fungi. We explored genomic variation in Sympodiorosea to assess potential alternative lifestyles, focusing on the diversity and evolution of metabolic genes. Our study revealed a constrained selective landscape across the Sympodiorosea genome. However, outcomes of in vitro host interactions were diverse and predictable based on the antagonist's ant-species-of-origin, suggesting functional diversification. Phylogenomics indicated that gene gain/loss events in carbohydrate-active enzymes and specialized metabolism drive this diversification. Although selection acts intensely on metabolism-related genes overall, specific metabolic genes experience diversifying selection, indicating their critical role in host associations. Furthermore, Sympodiorosea exhibits protease gene expansions and contractions discordant with a strictly mycoparasitic lifestyle, suggesting either an alternative lifestyle within ant gardens or recent evolution from other niches. These results provide novel insights into fungal genome evolution and the chemistry of the fungus-growing ant symbiosis.

items.title: BEAGLE 4.1: A high-performance library for computation on phylogenetic trees across diverse parallel architectures
items.summary: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations…

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: In 2023, an estimated 13% of worldwide deaths resulting from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were due to drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) documented a dramatic, sixfold increase in the number of patients treated with 6-month all-oral (BPaLM) regimens, from 5,653 patients in 2023, to 34,000 patients by 2024, while also documenting an emergence of bedaquiline resistance in real-world cohorts and a lack of efficacy of BCG revaccination in the BCG-PRIME Phase 2b trial against sustained Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Concurrently, the M72/AS01E subunit vaccine trial completed recruitment (approximately 20,000 individuals) across five high-burden countries, 11 months ahead of scheduled completion date. The first randomized controlled trial assessing DRTB-HDT host-directed therapy for DR-TB in adults (metformin + dovramilast), conducted at five international sites, is entering the late-stage readout phase. This synthesis of data, covering the period from 2015 through 2026, across six different dimensions includes molecular mechanisms of resistance, novel antimicrobial treatment modalities, host-directed therapy, immunity associated with regulatory compliance, adjuvants to vaccines, and the clinical translation of vaccine candidates. The Molecular-to-Translational continuum is used as a framework for the synthesis, with the regulatory immune function domain (T regulatory cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and check-point axes) linking all five domains. Our central hypothesis is that drug resistance evolution of the microbe and failure of the host to maintain regulatory immunity are interdependent and create a bidirectional relationship with each other. We have identified nine major research gaps, with milestone dates from 2026 to 2030, based on unresolved controversies regarding the bedaquiline resistance catalog and the acquisition versus transmission narrative.

items.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
items.summary: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on…

research.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT West Nile virus (WNV) is a flavivirus whose cycle involves mosquitoes and avian hosts that occasionally may infect horses and humans as “dead‐end hosts.” Human infection is mostly asymptomatic, sometimes leading to febrile or neuroinvasive disease. In 2025, Italy experienced its largest epidemic with an unprecedented geographic spread (79 provinces; 52% of cases in central Italy). Here we report whole‑genome sequencing and phylogeographic analysis of 39 WNV lineage 2 samples collected in Lazio and Campania regions between July and September 2025 from humans and animal samples. All 2025 strains belonged to a Southern Italian clade that diversified around 2020, with evidence of earlier circulation in 2024. All the 2025 genomes shared a substitution that lies in envelope protein domain III (K399R), potentially influencing interactions with the viral membrane. The same mutation was previously detected in Eastern European strains, leading to the hypothesis of introductions in Italy via migratory birds from these regions. Phylogeography identified strong viral dispersal routes within Central Italy supporting a pattern of short‑range spread and local overwintering. Overall, results highlight the roles of ecological conditions and cross‑border transmission dynamics in shaping the 2025 Italian epidemic, underscoring the need for integrated genomic/ecological surveillance.

research.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) results from acquiring mutations or genes that allow microbes to withstand antimicrobials. These genetic modifications can also cause non-selected changes in other cell phenotypes, such as fitness and susceptibility to antibiotic classes different from the one under selection. These collateral effects of AMR acquisition could be exploited to improve treatments. This is increasingly important in light of AMR as a major global health problem, associated with 4.71 million deaths worldwide in 2021, with 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to AMR. Additionally, the lack of development of novel antimicrobials active against resistant infections continues to compound the crisis. Even if new antimicrobials are developed, resistance will most likely emerge through adaptive evolution. Therefore, it is imperative to explore strategies to maintain the efficacy of new and existing antibiotics and limit the acquisition of AMR to continue to treat infections successfully. Understanding the impact of resistance acquisition on the bacterial phenotype, including collateral effects, has the potential to improve therapeutic outcomes. In this perspective, we will summarize the collateral effects of resistance acquisition, including fitness costs, collateral susceptibility networks, mutant selection windows and the probability of establishment of bacterial populations, and explore how these may be exploited to enhance the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. We will also discuss how challenges such as genetic background, polymicrobial infections and the environment are current barriers to the translation of these principles into the clinic.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 18 loci (L = 26,700 aligned columns; Lagomorpha outgroups, Sciuromorpha, Castorimorpha, Dipodoidea, invasive Muridae, and New World Cricetidae: Arvicolinae, Neotominae, and Sigmodontinae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three North American PopSets (Peromyscus maniculatus, Sigmodon hispidus, and Urocitellus parryii; 3 × N = 36 = 108 conspecific isolates) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The continental radiation of rodents (Order Rodentia) across North America via Paleogene Beringian corridors, Miocene grassland expansions, and Great American Biotic Interchange exchanges—coupled with the Anthropocene introduction of Old World commensal murids—established both the foundational small-mammal trophic guilds of Nearctic ecosystems and the primary sylvatic reservoirs for North America's major rodent-borne zoonoses. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across an 18-locus, 64-species Glires supermatrix (L = 26,700 aligned columns with 7,979 parsimony-informative sites and 8,803 distinct site patterns) paired with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three conspecific North American population datasets (3 × N = 36 = 108 isolates) benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors the Glires root (Lagomorpha vs. Rodentia) at 65.2 Ma, Crown Rodentia at 56.8 Ma, the Sciuromorpha–Castorimorpha split at 36.4 Ma, Myodonta (Dipodoidea vs. Muroidea) at 46.5 Ma, the Muridae–Cricetidae divergence at 24.8 Ma, Crown Cricetidae at 18.6 Ma, and the New World Neotominae–Sigmodontinae split at 13.4 Ma. Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on the Sin Nombre hantavirus endothelial receptor ITGB3 beta-3 integrin (omega = 0.5319), intermediate selective constraint on the high-altitude and fossorial hypoxia axis EPAS1/HBB (omega = 0.0343) and rodenticide-detoxification locus VKORC1/CYP2C (omega = 0.2572), and diversifying positive selection on bacterial pattern-recognition receptors TLR2/TLR4 (omega = 0.2631) and the New World Arenavirus receptor TFRC transferrin receptor 1 apical domain (omega = 0.1453). Across the three single-species PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve post-glacial forest/oak-mast expansion and contemporary ENSO Sin Nombre hantavirus / Lyme disease amplification in the North American deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus, N = 36, Ne = 433,194 to 653,847; *BEAST = 667,970), northward agricultural grassland expansion and Black Creek Canal / Tamiami viral irruptions in the hispid cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus, N = 36, Ne = 1,534,254 to 1,753,302; *BEAST = 1,808,005), and post-LGM Beringian steppe-tundra recolonization and high-latitude permafrost-thaw dynamics in the Arctic ground squirrel (Urocitellus parryii, N = 36, Ne = 707,606 to 1,687,680; *BEAST = 1,740,336), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 42.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.88 s vs. 595.24 s Hybrid and 1861.52 s full External UFBoot). research.abstract: AimsTo evaluate the effectiveness of GLP-1 RAs on clinical outcomes in diabetic patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Methods and resultsIn this retrospective observational cohort study, all adults with diabetes mellitus and HFrEF between 2014 and 2025 were identified. Patients treated with GLP-1 RAs were matched to controls using stratified exact matching. The primary outcome was a composite of heart failure hospitalization or all-cause mortality. Treatment effects were estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) to derive risk ratios, NNT estimates, and corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Time-to-event analyses using Cox proportional hazards models were performed as a validation analysis. Among 7,878 patients with HFrEF, 793 (10.1%) patients who initiated GLP-1 RA therapy after HF diagnosis were matched to 1,825 controls. GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with a lower risk of heart failure hospitalization or death, with risk ratios of 0.58 (95% CI: 0.42-0.77) at 12 months and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.61-0.85) at 36 months. The combination of high baseline event rates and substantial relative risk reduction translated into remarkably low NNT values in the overall population, with an NNT of 17 (95% CI: 11-33) at 1 year and 13 (95% CI: 8-25) at 3 years. Post hoc subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent effects across clinical subgroups, with no significant heterogeneity observed. ConclusionIn this large real-world cohort of diabetic patients with HFrEF, GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, in addition to guideline-directed medical therapy, was associated with a lower risk of death or heart failure hospitalization. items.summary: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A…

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. Our findings underscore the critical need to integrate WGS into TB surveillance and control programmes in Pakistan to guide targeted interventions and curb the spread of resistant strains. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62482-7.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila, and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

items.title: Experimental evolution reveals temporally opposing roles for Csu pili during Acinetobacter baumannii respiratory infection
items.summary: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections…

research.abstract: Abstract Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections observed in some patients. Recently, our laboratory developed a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection that enabled the identification of virulence factors specifically required for long-term lung persistence. To investigate how A. baumannii adapts during chronic pulmonary infection, we performed an experimental evolution study using this model. This approach revealed an unexpected role for the archaic chaperone-usher (Csu) pili in A. baumannii pathogenesis. At early time points, Csu expression reduced bacterial burdens in both acute and chronic pneumonia models, an effect associated with enhanced host inflammatory responses. In contrast, at later stages of chronic infection, Csu promoted bacterial persistence, potentially by facilitating adhesion to pulmonary epithelial cells. These opposing effects were conserved across two distinct A. baumannii clinical isolates. We also found that Csu contributes to bacterial colonization in a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) model in a strain-dependent manner. Together, these findings reveal an infection-stage-dependent role for Csu in A. baumannii pathogenesis, demonstrating that a bacterial surface structure can impair early colonization while promoting long-term persistence. Author summary Understanding how bacterial pathogens establish and maintain infections requires identifying the factors that promote their survival within the host. Currently, most experimental models of Acinetobacter baumannii infections focus on acute infections, potentially overlooking bacterial factors that are required for prolonged infections. In this study, we investigated how A. baumannii , a major cause of hospital-acquired infections, adapts to the lung environment during chronic infection. Using experimental evolution, we identified a novel role for Csu pili, surface structures traditionally associated with biofilm formation. Rather than promoting bacterial fitness throughout infection, Csu pili exhibited opposing effects depending on disease progression. Their expression was detrimental to bacterial fitness during early infection, a phenotype associated with increased host inflammatory responses, but became advantageous during prolonged infection, potentially by enhancing bacterial association with respiratory epithelial cells. Importantly, these opposing effects were observed in distinct clinical isolates, suggesting that this phenomenon is not restricted to a particular bacterial strain. Our findings highlight how the contribution of individual virulence factors can change over the course of infection and underscore the importance of considering infection duration when studying bacterial pathogenesis.

However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4…

research.abstract: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4 billion years ago (Ga) with fermentation and sulfur compound respiration. A second wave began ~3.2 Ga with aerobic respiration and growth, while a third began ~1.4 Ga with further specialization. We compared these predictions with independent dates from the geochemical record, and agreement with conservative dates was good (CCC = 0.81 to 0.89). Several forms of metabolism are invisible in the geochemical record, and our approach dates these forms, too. Our results reconcile different lines of evidence for microbial evolution and provide a fuller picture of early Earth.

research.abstract: Background: Predictive metabolomics enables efficient early cardiometabolic risk detection, supporting proactive prevention over traditional reactive healthcare approaches. We evaluated the impact of a novel metabolomic risk score (MRS)-based health check on healthcare workload and long-term cost-effectiveness compared with current practices in Finland's working-age population. Methods: A de novo individual-level microsimulation model was developed to estimate labour time and cost-effectiveness when identifying individuals at risk of cardiometabolic diseases (cardiovascular diseases; CVD or type 2 diabetes; T2D). The model used synthetic data on 256,372 Finnish individuals aged 50-54 years without prior CVD or T2D. From a societal perspective, three scenarios were assessed: 1) replacing the standard health checks with MRS-based health checks, 2) replacing standard health checks with MRS-based checks plus enhanced prevention, and 3) comparing enhanced standard checks with MRS-based checks plus enhanced prevention. Outcomes included time required to identify at-risk individuals, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio per QALY gained, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. Results: MRS-based health checks substantially reduce workload, saving 193,140 hours for nurses and 2,843 hours for physicians over five years. The approach is likely cost-saving across all scenarios, with discounted long-term savings ranging from EUR27 million to EUR258 million. In scenarios 1-2, QALYs improve, with gains from 1,316 to 10,813. In scenario 3, no QALY gains are observed, and minor losses occur due to differences in baseline risk stratification. Conclusions: MRS-based health checks in primary and occupational care reduce workload and are likely a cost-saving strategy with potential health outcome benefits in identifying individuals at risk of cardiometabolic diseases.

items.title: Decoding positive selection in Mycobacterium tuberculosis with phylogeny-guided graph attention models.
items.summary: MOTIVATION: Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a…

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a phylogeny-guided graph attention network approach, coupled with a novel method for converting SNP-annotated phylogenetic trees into graph structures suitable for graph neural network processing. Results Using a dataset of 1000 M. tuberculosis isolates, representing the four main lineages, and 206 single-nucleotide variants (75 resistance-associated and 131 neutral) spanning 79 drug-resistance genes, we constructed graphs where nodes represented individual isolates and edges reflected phylogenetic distances. To reduce noise and highlight local evolutionary structure, we pruned edges between isolates separated by more than seven internal nodes. Node features were encoded as binary indicators of SNP presence or absence, and the graph attention network (GAT) architecture comprised two attention layers with a residual connection, followed by global attention pooling and a multilayer perceptron classifier. The model achieved higher accuracy (0.81, AUC 0.82) than a homoplasy-count baseline (0.71) on the held-out test set. Under repeated cross-validation, however, F1 scores did not differ significantly (0.56 vs. 0.58; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.98), reflecting a specificity-sensitivity trade-off: the GAT favoured specificity (0.89), the baseline favoured sensitivity. Applying the model to 138 WHO-classified “uncertain” variants identified 28 high-confidence candidates, including rpoC Ile491Val (rifampicin, compensatory), ubiA Arg240Cys (ethambutol), and rpsA Ala412Val (pyrazinamide). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of encoding phylogenetic trees as graph neural network-compatible structures and the utility of attention-based models for detecting positive-selection signals, supporting genomic surveillance and prioritisation of candidates for experimental validation. Availability and Implementation The source code for the model can be found at https://github.com/linfeng-wang/Phylogeny-Guided_GAT .

research.abstract: Immunomodulatory Activity of Galing Leaf Extract and Fraction (Cayratia trifolia L) Against Specific Immune Response in ESAT-6 TB-Induced Diabetes Mellit us Rats The immune system protects the body against infections. However, in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM), impaired immune function increases the risk of developing active tuberculosis (TB). CD4+ T cell activation is essential for controlling Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, but immune system dysfunction in DM makes the body more susceptible to infection. Natural immunomodulators are promising therapeutic alternatives because they may have fewer side effects and can enhance immune responses. Galing (Cayratia trifolia L.) is known to contain bioactive compounds with antidiabetic, antibacterial, and immunomodulatory activities. This study aimed to investigate the potential of Galing leaf extract and fractions to enhance the CD4+-mediated specific immune response in an animal model of DM induced with the TB antigen ESAT-6. Dried plant material was macerated using 96% ethanol, followed by evaporation to obtain the ethanolic extract. Fractionation was then performed using vacuum liquid chromatography (VLC) with a gradient elution system, yielding five fractions. Immunomodulatory activity was evaluated by measuring CD4+ levels using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The experimental animals were divided into nine groups: normal control, negative control, positive control, fractions 1-5, and extract, with a dose of 50 mg/kg body weight administered to each treatment group. The immunomodulatory assay results showed CD4+ levels of 8.399 μg/mL in fraction 1, 8.047 μg/mL in fraction 2, 6.490 μg/mL in fraction 3, 6.492 μg/mL in fraction 4, 5.917 μg/mL in fraction 5, and 7.284 μg/mL in the extract group. The findings indicated that Galing leaf extract and fractions could enhance the specific immune response by increasing CD4+ levels. Galing demonstrated immunomodulatory activity, with fractions 1 and 2 showing the greatest efficacy (p < 0.05). In conclusion, Galing leaf extract and fractions have potential as natural immunomodulatory agents to enhance CD4+ mediated immune responses in an animal model of DM induced with the TB antigen ESAT-6. Sistem imun berfungsi melindungi tubuh dari infeksi. Namun, pada pasien diabetes melitus (DM), gangguan fungsi imun meningkatkan risiko terjadinya tuberkulosis (TB) aktif. Aktivasi sel T CD4+ sangat penting dalam mengendalikan infeksi Mycobacterium tuberculosis, tetapi gangguan sistem imun pada DM menyebabkan tubuh lebih rentan terhadap infeksi. Imunomodulator alami merupakan alternatif terapi yang menjanjikan karena memiliki efek samping yang lebih ringan dan dapat meningkatkan respons imun. Galing (Cayratia trifolia L.) diketahui mengandung senyawa bioaktif yang memiliki aktivitas antidiabetes, antibakteri, dan imunomodulator. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui potensi ekstrak dan fraksi daun galing dalam meningkatkan respons imun spesifik CD4+ pada model hewan DM yang diinduksi antigen TB ESAT-6. Serbuk tanaman kering dimaserasi menggunakan etanol 96% dan selanjutnya diuapkan untuk memperoleh ekstrak etanol. Selanjutnya, dilakukan fraksinasi menggunakan metode KVC dengan eluen bergradien sehingga diperoleh lima fraksi. Aktivitas imunomodulator dievaluasi dengan mengukur kadar CD4+ menggunakan metode ELISA. Hewan uji dibagi menjadi sembilan kelompok, yaitu kelompok normal, kontrol negatif, kontrol positif, fraksi 1, fraksi 2, fraksi 3, fraksi 4, fraksi 5, dan ekstrak, dengan dosis 50 mg/kg berat badan untuk masing-masing kelompok perlakuan. Hasil uji imunomodulator menunjukkan kadar CD4+ sebesar 8,399 μg/mL pada fraksi 1, 8,047 μg/mL pada fraksi 2, 6,490 μg/mL pada fraksi 3, 6,492 μg/mL pada fraksi 4, 5,917 μg/mL pada fraksi 5, dan 7,284 μg/mL pada kelompok ekstrak. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa ekstrak dan fraksi daun galing dapat meningkatkan respons imun spesifik melalui peningkatan (CD4+). Galing menunjukkan aktivitas imunomodulator, dengan fraksi 1 dan 2 menunjukkan aktivitas yang paling efektif (p < 0,05). Kesimpulannya, ekstrak dan fraksi daun galing berpotensi sebagai agen imunomodulator alami untuk meningkatkan respons imun yang dimediasi CD4+ pada model hewan DM yang diinduksi dengan antigen TB ESAT-6.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 16 loci (L = 23,924 aligned columns; African Catarrhini and Neotropical Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three independent PopSets (Alouatta spp., Sapajus/Cebus, and Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The colonization of South America by African anthropoid primates during the Middle to Late Eocene and their subsequent diversification across Neotropical forest strata into five ecologically specialized families (Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) represent one of mammalogy's classic trans-oceanic adaptive radiations. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across a 16-locus, 64-species primate supermatrix (L = 23,924 aligned columns with 10,254 parsimony-informative sites and 11,093 distinct site patterns) coupled with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three localized Neotropical population datasets benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors Crown Primates at 74.0 Ma, the trans-Atlantic Simiiformes split between African Catarrhini (crown 28.5 Ma) and Neotropical Platyrrhini at 43.2 Ma (stem rafting window 43.2–24.2 Ma across the Eocene Atlantic), and Crown Platyrrhini at 24.2 Ma, followed by crown radiations of Pitheciidae (19.8 Ma), Atelidae (16.8 Ma), Cebidae (19.5 Ma), Callitrichidae (14.8 Ma), and Aotidae (11.4 Ma). Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on Pro8-oxytocin OXT/OXTR neuroendocrine signaling (omega = 0.4905), intermediate selective constraint on TAS2R bitter-taste receptors (omega = 0.7442) and ENAM/GHR dental and phyletic-dwarfism loci (omega = 0.8436), and diversifying and balancing selection on duplicated RNASE1/CHIA folivory-insectivory digestive enzymes (omega = 1.2118) and X-linked OPN1LW spectral-tuning opsin exons (omega = 2.4891). Across the three localized PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve late Quaternary trans-Andean expansion and contemporary yellow fever epizootic pressure in howler monkeys (Alouatta, Ne = 628,056 to 977,186; *BEAST = 1,007,674), Pleistocene Cerrado/Caatinga dry-corridor colonization and stone-tool nut-cracking persistence in capuchins (Sapajus/Cebus, Ne = 1,042,598 to 1,376,278; *BEAST = 1,411,397), and Atlantic Forest fragmentation followed by metapopulation translocation recovery in callitrichid marmosets and tamarins (Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus, Ne = 469,859 to 912,085; *BEAST = 940,542), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 29.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.54 s vs. 404.82 s Hybrid and 3127.88 s full External UFBoot). research.abstract: Abstract Background The HSP70 family maintains cellular proteostasis and mediates vertebrate responses to environmental stress. The Chinese alligator ( Alligator sinensis ), an ectothermic crocodilian, undergoes winter dormancy characterized by cessation of feeding, reduced activity, and metabolic depression. However, the evolutionary patterns of the HSP70 family across vertebrates and their potential relevance to winter dormancy in crocodilians remain poorly understood. We characterized the HSP70 family across 24 vertebrate species, focusing on the molecular evolution of HSPA12A along crocodilian lineages and its seasonal expression in the hypothalamus of the Chinese alligator. Results Using HMMER- and BLAST-based searches, we identified 355 HSP70 family members, with 11–28 members per species. Phylogenetic, synteny, and subcellular localization analyses indicated that the family is broadly conserved but exhibits subfamily- and lineage-associated divergence. Under two foreground schemes in which the terminal branches of two winter-dormant crocodilians or all four crocodilian species were jointly designated as foreground, HSPA12A showed an elevated relative evolutionary rate and significant evidence of positive selection. HyPhy aBSREL supported episodic diversifying selection on the A. sinensis HSPA12A terminal branch. Public RNA-seq data showed that HSPA12A expression was highest in the hypothalamus among sampled female tissues and was higher in winter than in summer (600.0 and 329.2 TPM, respectively). Western blotting and immunofluorescence analyses showed descriptive differences between the examined specimens, with higher HSPA12A protein abundance and a higher density of cells double-positive for anti-HSPA12A antibody immunoreactivity and NeuN in winter. Because each RNA-seq, western blotting, and immunofluorescence comparison included only one biological specimen per season, these observations were treated as descriptive, and no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Conclusions The vertebrate HSP70 family is broadly conserved but shows differentiation among subfamilies and lineages. The evolutionary analyses indicate a broader crocodilian-lineage-associated pattern of HSPA12A evolution that cannot be attributed specifically to winter dormancy. Separately, the descriptive transcriptomic and preliminary protein-level observations provide a basis for considering HSPA12A as a candidate for further investigation in relation to winter physiology in the Chinese alligator. These findings do not establish winter dormancy as the selective driver of HSPA12A evolution, and its biological function and causal role remain to be determined.

research.abstract: **Abstract** **Background** Young adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D) in low- and middle-income countries experience persistently poor glycaemic control despite improved insulin access. Evidence on the effects of social determinants of health (SDOH) on glycaemic control, complications, and psychological well-being remains limited, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. We examined relationships between SDOH, psychological health, glycaemic control, and early complication markers among young adults with T1D in Kenya. **Methods** We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among 164 adults aged 18-34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. SDOH were assessed using a prespecified, context-informed questionnaire covering six domains. Psychological well-being was assessed using PAID, PHQ-9, and GAD-7. Clinical outcomes included HbA1c, a single urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and lipid profile. Associations between SDOH domains and clinical and psychological outcomes were evaluated using multivariable ordinal and binary logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, and diabetes duration. **Findings** Mean age was 24.96+/-4.35 years and diabetes duration 7.26+/-5.70 years. Mean HbA1c was 11.5+/-3.44%, with only 4.9% achieving <7%. LDL cholesterol was above target in 56.1%, 64.0% had an elevated LDL/HDL ratio, and 28.0% had elevated UACR. Diabetes distress and clinically significant depressive symptoms affected 30.5% and 27.5%, respectively. Moderate-to-high SDOH burden was greatest for economic stability (76.8%), social/community context (52.4%), and food environment (43.9%). All SDOH domains showed positive but non-significant associations with HbA1c. Diabetes distress was associated with economic instability (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.17-1.72), healthcare system burden (1.45, 1.12-1.87), neighbourhood/physical environment burden (1.39, 1.07-1.80), and food environment burden (1.30, 1.03-1.64). Anxiety was associated with social/community (1.70, 1.14-2.53) and healthcare system burden (1.68, 1.19-2.36). Economic instability was associated with elevated UACR (1.40, 1.05-1.85). **Discussion** Young adults with T1D in Kenya experience substantial social and psychological burden alongside poor glycaemic control and early complication markers. Social disadvantage appears to influence kidney disease complications, and psychological well-being regardless of glycaemic control in our sample, underscoring the need to move beyond glucose-centered care. Poor glycaemic control was pervasive, which likely obviated any detectable differences by SDOH in this population. Ultimately, Integrated care addressing SDOH and mental health may support more sustainable long-term outcomes. Key words: Type 1 diabetes; Social determinants; glycemic control; complications, psychological health

research.abstract: Abstract Mussels belonging to the genus Mytilus are among the world’s most ecologically and economically important bivalve molluscs. Although the genus most likely originated in the Northern Hemisphere, the evolutionary history of Southern Hemisphere lineages, including the timing and number of colonisation events leading to the extant Australian populations, remains debated. Limited genomic resources have hindered the reconstruction of these evolutionary histories. In Australia, distinguishing native Mytilus planulatus from invasive Mytilus galloprovincialis is critical for biosecurity and conservation, but previous molecular approaches lacked sufficient resolution to resolve species boundaries and hybridisation patterns. Here, we present the first chromosome-scale reference genome for M. planulatus . The assembly consists of 14 chromosomes and over 51,000 annotated protein-coding genes per haplotype. Comparative analysis revealed extensive structural variation and widespread hemizygosity despite a largely conserved chromosomal organisation relative to M. galloprovincialis . Population analyses using SNPs and gene presence-absence variation in resequenced individuals confirmed previously inferred patterns of population structure and establish this reference genome as a valuable resource for future studies of genome evolution, adaptation and population genomics in Mytilus .

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Neovascular tufts (NVTs) are a defining feature of proliferative retinopathies such as diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity, in which they compromise retinal integrity and vision. Excessive endothelial cell (EC) sprouting underlies their formation, yet the cellular and mechanical mechanisms that shape NVTs, and the contribution of pericytes (PCs) to this process, remain unclear. In this work, we investigated the role of actomyosin contractility in ECs and PCs during pathological angiogenesis and NVT formation. We identified non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) and phosphorylated myosin light chains (MLCs) as a key signature of PCs and ECs in retinopathy and NVTs. Using inducible deletion of Myh9 in the oxygen-induced retinopathy mouse model, we uncover distinct and opposing roles for NMIIA in the two cell types. Endothelial NMIIA promotes neovascularisation and prevents enlargement of NVTs, whilst PC NMIIA drives neovascular tuft formation. Mechanistically, we identify platelet-derived growth factor D (PDGFD), but not PDGFB, as a driver of pathological PC actomyosin contractility through Rho-associated coiled-coil kinase (ROCK). Genetic deletion of Pdgfd partially phenocopies the loss of NMIIA in PCs, reducing NVT formation and lowering NMIIA and phosphorylated MLC levels within NVTs. Our findings establish cell-type-specific actomyosin contractility as a determinant of NVT pathogenesis and identify PDGFD-ROCK-NMIIA signalling in PCs as a therapeutic target in proliferative retinopathies.

research.abstract: Abstract Purpose We introduce GraNPA (Graph Node-Phenotype Association), a method that performs a phenotype-sequence association analysis on a pangenome variation graph (PVG). This PVG is built using a small number of individual genome sequences and does not require additional population materials or kinship information for qualitative phenotypes. This approach minimizes the number of individuals required for association studies and mitigates the impact of reference bias in variant calling within these types of analyses. Background A PVG is a representation of the multiple alignment of a set of complete genomes. It contains all variations, ranging from single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to large structural variations (SVs), and these are represented as nodes in the graph. By integrating phenotype information within these nodes, we can assign a Score ( S ) to each one and identify regions related to the phenotype directly within the PVG. These regions represent statistically significant shifts in S distribution, indicating their involvement in the phenotype. Finally, GraNPA provides their positions and scores for further analysis. Results This method was tested using different simulated contexts and two publicly available datasets: the Sub1A gene locus for Asian rice Oryza sativa in a 13 individuals PVG, and the insertion responsible for the white-headed in cattle ( Bos taurus ) with a PVG of 24 individuals. Source code of GraNPA is available here https://forge.ird.fr/diade/graphgwas/granpa under GNU GPLv3. Conclusion GraNPA was able to identify the expected area in two simulated datasets, as well as the loci responsible for these two known traits, using only a few dozen complete genomes from these PVGs. Although this method is currently limited to qualitative phenotypes, it paves the way for more efficient methods that rely on PVGs and a small number of individuals.

research.abstract: Abstract Deep-sea hydrothermal vents and methane seeps host unique animal communities sustained by chemosynthetic symbioses, yet how biological diversification proceeds across these geochemically distinct and geographically fragmented habitats remains poorly understood. Previous studies have largely focused on either host genomic adaptation or symbiont diversity as drivers of isolation, leaving unresolved how environmental geochemistry and host–microbe associations jointly shape evolutionary trajectories in chemosynthetic ecosystems. Here, we addressed this gap by combining chromosome-level host genomics, population resequencing, and episymbiont metagenomics in the deep-sea chemosynthetic lobster Shinkaia crosnieri, a dominant species inhabiting both hydrothermal vents and methane seeps. Genomic innovations—including sensory tradeoffs (vision loss versus chemosensory expansion), metabolic compensation for pigment loss, and positive selection on respiratory protein—underpin deep-sea colonization of S. crosnieri. Populations from the Okinawa Trough vent and the South China Sea seep exhibit pronounced genetic divergence, potentially driven by Pleistocene vicariance and reinforced by divergent selection across sulfur-enriched (vent) versus sulfur-depleted, methane-dominated (seep) environments. This selection targets host genes involved in chemoreception and immunity, with coordinated signatures in both sequence evolution and structural variation. Crucially, holobiont-level adaptation is amplified by habitat-specific recruitment of episymbionts: sulfur-oxidizing Campylobacterales/Thiotrichales dominate vent-associated lobsters, while methanotrophic Methylococcales prevail at seep counterparts. These symbionts partition energy niches metabolically, with seep-associated communities enhancing biosynthesis of key cofactors (e.g. coenzyme Q, tetrahydrofolate). Host transporters for these nutrients are concurrently upregulated, demonstrating functional synergy. Our findings establish that diversification in extreme environments operates holobiont-wide, where geochemical gradients synergistically shape host genomic plasticity and symbiont metabolic specialization to drive early-stage divergence.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT China's complex river basins constitute a critical biogeographic setting for investigating genetic differentiation and lineage divergence in freshwater fishes. Opsariichthys bidens is broadly distributed among multiple, hydrologically isolated river basins, rendering it a well‐suited system for assessing mitochondrial phylogeographic structure across major river basins. Here, we used newly generated mitochondrial data to characterize broad‐scale genetic variation in O. bidens across China's major river basins. We analyzed 379 cytochrome b ( cyt b ) sequences sampled from 13 geographically distinct populations, including seven populations from the Yangtze River and one population from each of six other major rivers, complemented by complete mitochondrial genomes from one individual from each population. Mitochondrial diversity was high at the species level (haplotype diversity, H d = 0.942; nucleotide diversity, π = 0.02526), but varied markedly among populations, with some populations showing haplotype fixation and others retaining divergent haplotypes. Genetic differentiation was pronounced, with 83.84% of variation attributable to differences among populations; 93.6% of pairwise F st values exceeded 0.25. Haplotype‐network and phylogenetic analyses showed two deeply divergent mitochondrial lineages, broadly distributed in northern and southern China, respectively, with further substructure broadly associated with major river basins. Complete mitochondrial genomes exhibited high structural conservation across lineages, and the clearest lineage‐associated annotation differences were observed in the termination codons of nd1 and cox3 . Overall, these results provide a broad‐scale mitochondrial phylogeographic assessment of O. bidens and reveal a general association between river‐basin geography and mitochondrial lineage structure across China.

research.abstract: Abstract The evolution of pesticide resistance in herbivores poses a significant challenge in agriculture. A refuge strategy, where farmers plant non-toxin-treated plants to promote growth of susceptible herbivore individuals near treated plants and facilitate gene exchange between susceptible and resistant individuals, has been used in resistance management. However, we know very little about the effect of spatiotemporal fluctuations in selection pressure on resistance management. Furthermore, pests show oviposition preference and assortative mating behaviours, both of which have rarely been considered by researchers when designing resistance management strategies. Using a stochastic eco-evolutionary plant-herbivore model, we show that over a wide range of population parameters, directional changes in toxicity level and refuge frequency that reduce selection pressure for the resistance allele in the initial pest generations are much more effective for resistance management than exposing pests to a constant toxicity level and refuge frequency across pest generations. However, the exact magnitude of the effect of changing toxicity and refuge frequency relative to keeping them constant across pest generations is sensitive to underlying population parameter values. Our results show that the refuge strategy is most effective when niche choice can evolve, but assortative mating shows both negative and positive effects in resistance management. Thus, our results reveal a potential mechanism underlying the refuge strategy’s successes in the field. We show how resistance allele dominance and resistance costs influence our observations, and discuss our results in the context of partial protection from directional selection and field resistance management.

research.abstract: Networks are widely used to represent relationships among features (e.g. genes, proteins, and microbial taxa) and among observations (e.g. cells, samples, and species) in omics data, as well as their neighborhoods. The Bioconductor ecosystem provides users and developers with modular and interoperable software tools by relying on standard data structures that are reused across packages. However, Bioconductor lacks a standard data structure to store such networks together with the quantitative data from which they are inferred. Here, we present GraphExperiment , an R/Bioconductor package that provides an S4 class extending SingleCellExperiment with containers for feature-level ( rowGraphs ) and observation-level ( colGraphs ) networks stored as igraph objects. Networks are kept in sync with assays, row and column metadata, allowing the simultaneous manipulation of quantitative data and graphs. We demonstrate GraphExperiment in seven use cases covering bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics, microbiome, and comparative genomics data, with networks ranging from gene coexpression and protein co-abundance networks to cell-cell communication and phylogenetic networks. GraphExperiment is available on Bioconductor ( https://bioconductor.org/packages/GraphExperiment ).

research.abstract: Abstract Sequence-to-function (S2F) deep learning models predict genome-wide functional profiles directly from DNA sequences and have significantly advanced our understanding of gene regulation. However, existing S2F models are fundamentally constrained by their initial training datasets, and no single model encompasses the full spectrum of cell types, clinical conditions, and cellular states, while training new models de novo is nontrivial. Here, we develop Kidzoi, a kidney cell-type-specific S2F model obtained by transfer learning from the pretrained model Borzoi using single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from human kidney tissue. Kidzoi accurately predicts cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and improves regulatory variant effect prediction in proximal tubule cells by up to 23% in terms of AUROC over existing models. Furthermore, Kidzoi effectively prioritizes genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapped causal variants associated with kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate based on both creatinine and cystatin C; eGFRcr-cys) while resolving their cell-type specificity. Systematic ablation of flanking sequence indicates that a local context of 32–64 kbp , representing only 6–12% of the full model input, captures most of the information needed for variant effect prediction. Finally, we show that a multi-task model achieves comparable performance to single-task models at a substantially reduced computational cost.

research.abstract: Tsaoko stripe mosaic virus (TkSMV) has been identified as the predominant viral pathogen of Amomum tsaoko in Yunnan Province of China. This virus induced various foliar symptoms, including chlorosis, stripe mosaic, and necrosis, while some infected A. tsaoko plants remain asymptomatic. Comprehensive investigation of the population genetic structure and molecular detection protocols for TkSMV is crucial for elucidating its evolutionary dynamics, epidemiology, and disease control strategies. Phylogenetic analysis based on 15 full-length genomic sequences and 29 coat protein (CP) gene fragments revealed three distinct evolutionary lineages (S1, S2, and S3) within the TkSMV population. Neutrality test analysis indicates that the genetic polymorphism of the TkSMV population is consistent with a neutral evolution model (Tajima’s D > 0, not significant). The comparative evolutionary analysis demonstrated significant selective pressures across viral proteins: codon usage bias analysis revealed strong purifying selection (dN/dS < 1) in nine structural/functional proteins, eliminating deleterious mutations. The 9K gene exhibited the highest nucleotide diversity (π = 0.13567), suggesting its role in adaptive evolution. NIa-Pro protease showed the lowest diversity (π = 0.09497), indicating functional constraint. Remarkably, the CP gene displayed polarized evolutionary patterns. The N-terminal region (amino acids 1 to 100) acted as a hypervariable hotspot, while the C-terminal region (amino acids 151 to 240) maintained evolutionary conservation. Furthermore, multiplex RT-PCR assays for accurate discrimination of TkSMV-S1/S2/S3 strains in mixed infections were developed. These advancements provide a technical foundation for epidemiological surveillance through strain-specific monitoring and seed certification programs for A. tsaoko cultivation.

research.abstract: Background Anterior chest wall tuberculosis is an uncommon form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that can mimic a chronic pyogenic abscess or chest wall mass. Its indolent presentation and absence of constitutional symptoms may delay diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings. Case presentation A 22-year-old previously healthy male soldier presented with a progressively enlarging parasternal-xiphoid swelling and intermittent seropurulent discharge, without respiratory or constitutional symptoms. Examination revealed a minimally tender 5 × 2 cm fluctuant swelling with a draining sinus and localized skin changes. Thoracic computed tomography showed a 57 × 18 mm subcutaneous collection at the xiphoid level without demonstrated pleural or osseous involvement, alongside centrilobular nodules and a tree-in-bud pattern suggestive of pulmonary infection. Incision, drainage, and debridement were performed. Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing of a fluid specimen detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex at a low bacillary load, without rifampicin resistance detected. Histopathological examination was reported to show caseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Sputum testing was also positive for M. tuberculosis, supporting concomitant pulmonary tuberculosis. First-line antituberculous therapy was initiated. The wound was closed at the 14-day postoperative assessment. Following six months of treatment, the patient remained asymptomatic; follow-up computed tomography demonstrated resolution of the chest wall collection and regression of pulmonary abnormalities. Conclusion Chest wall tuberculosis should be considered in patients with persistent parasternal swelling or a draining sinus, even without constitutional or respiratory symptoms. Tissue sampling, molecular and histopathological evaluation, and assessment for concomitant pulmonary disease support timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently co-occur, but the contributions of shared genetic susceptibility and directional associations remain unclear. Methods We analyzed European-ancestry GWAS summary statistics for ADHD (38,691 cases; 186,843 controls) and BPD (12,339 cases; 1,041,717 controls). Linkage disequilibrium score regression, conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), MR-LAP, CAUSE, colocalization, and SuSiE fine-mapping assessed genetic overlap and directional associations. Results ADHD and BPD showed substantial genetic correlation (r_g = 0.733). ConjFDR identified 48 shared loci, of which 36 (75%) showed consistent effect directions across independent phenotype-specific comparisons. Functional annotation highlighted axon guidance, oxidative phosphorylation, and a developing midbrain cell-type signature. ADHD-to-BPD MR supported a positive association (22 instruments; IVW-β = 0.487, SE = 0.082, p = 3.27 × 10⁻⁹), persisting after outlier removal, MR-LAP correction, and exclusion of two instruments indexing colocalized loci. Reverse MR was also positive (five instruments; IVW-β = 0.303, SE = 0.112, p = 6.83 × 10⁻³), but showed heterogeneity and sensitivity to individual variants. CAUSE favored directional over sharing-only models for ADHD-to-BPD (ΔELPD = 6.98; p = 7.3 × 10⁻⁸) and BPD-to-ADHD (ΔELPD = 5.92; p = 6.2 × 10⁻⁵). Colocalization and SuSiE supported shared signals at loci indexed by rs17576773 and rs9969232 for ADHD-to-BPD and rs4727799 in the reverse direction. Conclusions ADHD and BPD share extensive genetic susceptibility. Although CAUSE favored directional models in both directions, evidence across MR approaches was more consistent for ADHD-to-BPD. Shared genetic mechanisms and residual pleiotropy limit causal interpretation.

research.abstract: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

research.abstract: Background Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal–lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. Methods During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. Results Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. Discussion Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract In April-July 2026, Andes virus (ANDV) caused an outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths. Before symptom onset, the index case had travelled through hantavirus-endemic regions of Chile and Argentina, leaving the geographic origin of infection unresolved. We conducted phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses using newly generated ANDV genomes from human cases and rodent reservoirs to investigate the likely origin of the outbreak. Through phylogenetic analyses, we show that the outbreak genome falls within a geographically structured lineage spanning southern Chile and Argentine Andean Patagonia. Using phylogeographic reconstructions across all three segments, integrated with the index case’s travel itinerary, we identified the Toltén-Lanco area of southern Chile as the most likely geographic origin of the outbreak genome, with two candidate locations accounting for >98% of the posterior support. However, the index case visited this area 62-66 days before symptom onset, exceeding the conventionally reported ANDV incubation period of 7-42 days. Thus, while genomic evidence supports a southern Chilean origin of the outbreak genome, the timing and circumstances of transmission to the index case remain unresolved.

research.abstract: The intersection of tuberculosis (TB) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a major global health challenge. Although T2DM is a recognized risk factor for active TB, its epidemiological impact on latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and the underlying immune mechanisms remain unclear. This meta-analysis estimated the global prevalence of LTBI in T2DM, compared LTBI risk with non-diabetic controls, and evaluated the roles of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) in immune dysregulation. HbA1c and IFN-γ were selected because they represent the gold-standard indicators of long-term glycemic control and IGRA-based immune responses, respectively. A systematic search identified observational studies using interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) to diagnose LTBI in T2DM patients. Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation was performed to calculate pooled prevalence, odds ratios (ORs), mean differences (MDs) for HbA1c, and standardized mean differences (SMDs) for IFN-γ levels. Ten studies involving 1,740 T2DM patients and non-diabetic controls were included. The pooled LTBI prevalence in T2DM was 27% (95% CI: 23%–32%; I² = 76%). Compared with non-diabetic individuals, T2DM patients had an 86% higher risk of LTBI (OR 1.86; 95% CI: 1.41–2.45; p<0.0001; I² = 0%). T2DM patients with LTBI also showed poorer glycemic control, with HbA1c levels 0.75% higher than those without LTBI (MD 0.75; 95% CI: 0.51–0.99; p<0.00001; I² = 0%). Furthermore, T2DM was associated with significantly reduced Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific IFN-γ production (SMD −1.93; 95% CI: −2.69 to −1.16; p<0.00001; I² = 78%). These findings indicate that T2DM substantially increases LTBI risk through hyperglycemia-associated immune dysregulation and impaired Th1-mediated IFN-γ responses. Routine LTBI screening using IGRA and optimal glycemic control should be integrated into diabetes management to reduce progression to active TB. Keywords: : latent tuberculosis infection, type 2 diabetes mellitus, HbA1c, interferon-gamma, meta-analysis

research.abstract: Abstract Human milk contains a diverse array of metabolites that contribute to infant nutrition, immune development, and microbial colonization. The maternal factors shaping the milk metabolome, and the relative contribution of genetics or diet vs. other factors, remain poorly understood. Here, we profiled 458 milk metabolites in 349 one-month postpartum human milk samples and integrated metabolomic data with maternal diet, clinical, transcriptomic, and genomic measurements. Maternal diet was broadly associated with milk metabolite composition, with significant correlations identified between dietary features and 323 metabolites. Coffee consumption strongly predicted milk quinic acid and 1,3-dimethyluric acid abundance, while high-fiber dietary patterns were associated with metabolites including proline-betaine and N-acetylornithine. Integration of milk transcriptomic and metabolomic data via machine learning identified biologically plausible gene-metabolite pairs, including associations between QPRT expression and quinolinic acid, and DPEP1 and cysteine-glycine dipeptide. Genome-wide association analyses identified nine study-wide significant metabolite quantitative trait loci, including novel milk-specific associations near PDE6A affecting purine metabolites and near GNE affecting free sialic acid. Comparison with plasma metabolite studies demonstrated both shared and milk-specific genetic regulation of metabolites. Finally, we found that of all tested maternal features, diet explained the largest proportion of variation in the milk metabolome. Together, these findings demonstrate that the human milk metabolome reflects both maternal exposures and mammary gland-specific biology. This work establishes a framework for understanding how genetic and environmental factors shape milk composition.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Deciphering the genomic and enzymatic features associated with high-abundance specialized metabolism is important for understanding and engineering bioactive natural product biosynthesis. Asperosaponin VI, a hederagenin-based saponin, accumulates at exceptionally high levels in Dipsacus asperoides roots and is by far the predominant triterpenoid saponin. Here, by integrating a chromosome-level genome assembly with comparative genomics, transcriptomics, metabolite profiling, and biochemical characterization, we reconstructed a major biosynthetic route to asperosaponin VI and identified diversification of triterpenoid-associated gene families. Functional analyses revealed an ordered glycosylation sequence in which DaUGT73GZ2 preferentially accepts C-3-glycosylated substrates retaining a free C-28 carboxyl group, thereby establishing a C-3-before-C-28 glycosylation order during asperosaponin VI biosynthesis. Phylogenetic and biochemical analyses further uncovered functional differentiation among UGT85CA enzymes involved in C-3 arabinosylation, while genomic and expression analyses revealed lineage-specific patterns of pathway gene duplication and transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify genomic, enzymatic, and transcriptional features associated with the distinctive, high-abundance triterpenoid saponin profile of D. asperoides roots and provide a framework for understanding and engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis. Short Summary Integrated genomic and biochemical analyses of Dipsacus asperoides link the predominant accumulation of asperosaponin VI to gene duplication, glycosyltransferase diversification, ordered glycosylation, and root-biased expression. These findings connect genome evolution with specialized metabolic output and identify genes and enzymes useful for engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis.

research.abstract: Abstract Ancestral sequences and substitution histories are usually averaged out in phylogenetic inference and are therefore not reported to the user. However, they can be recovered through ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) and stochastic character mapping. By implementing and validating a new ASR and stochastic mapping package compatible with both single-locus and multispecies coalescent analysis, we show how reconstructing substitution histories can enhance the information gained about the tempo and mode of molecular evolution. We observe that known substitution histories (simulated and empirical) are recovered more accurately and precisely on time trees compared with unconstrained and non-ultrametric substitution trees that lack temporal directionality (maximum likelihood and Bayesian). We show that codon-partition models with site-rate heterogeneity, based on the four nucleotide characters, can effectively approximate the histories of synonymous and non-synonymous change, while requiring far less runtime than computationally demanding codon models that require 61 characters. In turn, this provides low-bias estimation of dN/dS that is robust to non-stationarity in GC content, codon usage bias, and nucleotide exchangeability rates. Lastly, using three case studies, we demonstrate how the approach can recover expected patterns in molecular evolution and pathogen transmission: that i) smaller-bodied mammalian species tend to have faster synonymous substitution rates than larger relatives, ii) amino acid substitutions are correlated with 3Di structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and iii) influenza A virus spread more frequently to nearby locations than distant ones, in a major H3N2 outbreak in New Zealand. These three trends were more pronounced when based on count estimates derived from stochastic mapping, relative to parametric rates and distances. Our open-source code comes with a user-friendly graphical interface, as the BeastMap package for BEAST 2; supporting a wide range of clock, site, and tree models and data types – including insertions and deletions – within a Bayesian phylogenetic framework.

research.abstract: Abstract Freshwater biodiversity is declining at alarming rates, and the biological characteristics of small freshwater fishes make them particularly vulnerable to habitat degradation and fragmentation. Pygmy perches are small Australian fishes whose populations have recently undergone rapid declines due to human-induced pressures. They also exhibit paedomorphic miniaturization, an evolutionary phenomenon whose consequences for the persistence and diversification of freshwater fishes remain unclear. Genomic resources for pygmy perches would significantly enhance both conservation efforts and evolutionary research. Here, we describe chromosome-level genome assemblies for the Southern pygmy perch (Nannoperca australis) and the Yarra pygmy perch (N. obscura). We provide evidence for high synteny among percichthyid genomes and for positive selection on size- and growth-related genes in the pygmy perch lineage. The N. australis and N. obscura assemblies are 675.7 and 653.9 Mbp in length, with scaffold N50 values of 26.98 and 26.22 Mbp, respectively. Each assembly comprises 24 pseudo-chromosomes and 890 or 1,476 contigs, with repeat contents of 22.3% and 28.1%. We predicted 26,390 and 24,654 protein-coding genes, and BUSCO completeness scores for Teleostei genes were 96.9% and 96.5%, respectively, for N. australis and N. obscura. Their genomes are comparable in quality to the best currently available percichthyid assemblies. These genomic resources will support conservation management efforts and provide a foundation for comparative studies on the adaptive significance of miniaturization.
